newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. doctors improvise to make up for rare organs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. doctors improvise to make up for rare organs.

text.p: Haden Thomas was just four months old when doctors told his parents he could die unless he received a new liver.

Haden, who was born with liver disease and already had undergone surgery for jaundiced skin, was put on a waiting list for a liver. After a year of waiting, his parents, Nanette and Lynn Thomas, decided on a rare procedure, donating half of his father's healthy liver to his tiny son.
"It was a big decision," Nanette Thomas, 29, said. "My husband was so afraid it wasn't going to work for Haden."

It took doctors seven hours to remove half of Lynn Thomas' liver and another 12 hours to transplant it in Haden. But the procedure, known as a living-related transplant, paid off. Haden, now 18 months old, is home in Tompkinsville, Kentucky. His father, 38, is doing well and doctors said the missing half of his liver will grow back quickly.

The family's experience spotlights one of the rare procedures doctors are using to save transplant patients, given the shortage of donor organs and a system for distributing them that, some experts charge, does not take care of the sickest patients first.

Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala is expected to issue regulations concerning liver allocation within a few months, after hearings last December in which transplant experts made the case for a national distribution system.

"The policies in place now do not represent patient concerns," Dr. John Fung, chief of the transplant surgery division at University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC), said. "We're not going to increase the number of donors until we address the unfairness of the system."
COMPLICATED SYSTEM FOR ORGAN DONATIONS

Donor livers, hearts, and other organs are distributed under a federal contract by United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), a Richmond, Virginia-based organization comprised of officials from transplant centers, health and medical organizations, members of the general public and organ procurement centers.

When organs become available, they are collected in local regions and first offered to patients within those regions. There are 69 of these regions in the United States. Only when a compatible recipient is not available locally is an organ offered to a patient in one of 11 larger regions. If no compatible patient is waiting there, the organ is offered nationally.
As a result, medical experts said, a liver that becomes available in Connecticut would go to a recipient there before one in Kentucky even if the Kentucky patient was much sicker.

Fung said organs should be offered nationally so the sickest patients receive them first. He said national allocation would work for livers because they can be preserved up to 24 hours, unlike other organs such as hearts with shorter life spans.
"There's no reason a liver in Pittsburgh can't be flown to Hawaii overnight if that is where the sickest patient is," he said. He said only 4 percent of livers are shared nationally.
DONOR LIVERS DISCARDED
Fung said some donor livers that could be used to save lives are discarded in the local regions but a study has never been done to determine why this happens.

According to UPMC, the world's largest transplant center, 7,000 people in the United States are waiting for livers, several hundred of whom will die this year without receiving one. About 4,000 liver transplants are performed each year.

As a result of the liver shortage, Fung said, doctors are performing more living-related transplants and also are splitting livers from deceased donors in half for two recipients. But the procedures are still rare and UNOS has no system in place to encourage doctors to learn them, he said.
About 50 living-related and a similar number of split-liver transplants were performed in the United States last year.

Officials at UNOS acknowledged the current allocation system could be modified but said national distribution would not save more lives. "It won't transplant as many patients per year on a net basis," Dr. James Burdick, UNOS president and a transplant surgeon at Johns Hopkins Medical Center, said. He said 30 percent of available livers were offered nationally, many times more than the figure cited by Fung.
ALLOCATION SYSTEM FAULTED

Burdick said the problem was a shortage of donors, not the allocation system. "There is no allocation system that will allow us to get out from under that," he said. He also said some livers were discarded because they were unsuitable for transplant.
"Most people in the field would agree that it's because the livers are unhealthy," he said.

Nat Semple, chairman of public policy for Transplant Recipients International Organization, a patient advocacy group, said UNOS does not want to change the allocation system because it protects transplant centers in local regions that otherwise may not receive financial compensation.
"A liver transplant can bring a hospital in excess of $300,000," he said. He said the problem will only get worse as more people are covered under managed health care.
"People will be told where to go for a transplant, they won't be able to choose," he said. "If organs don't follow patients, patients could be sent to their deaths."
